en: Oṃ. Salutations to the venerable gurus; salutations to the venerable Sundaragaṇapati.

• Dots (…) are used to indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters; • there are generally four to five lines on each side.
• Roman numerals such as (1), (2),
(3) denote the image number and line number.
• Devanāgarī numerals such as (1), (2), (3) [denote the same].
This indicates the *śloka* number.
*Hariḥ oṃ*—may there be auspiciousness (*śubham astu*).
O Caṇḍeśvara, you who are embraced by the supreme lotus-like face of Nīlakaṇṭha, grant me the fruit of Śambhu’s grace; salutations to you!
One should eat the remains of the offerings... by the command of Śiva.
(2) One should not revile the causal Deity, nor the scripture spoken by Him;
(3) nor the Guru, nor the practitioner, nor should one step over the shadow of the Liṅga.
One initiated by Śiva should neither step over nor give away the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
(i. 5b) — May there be auspiciousness; [this is] the *Aṣṭaka*.
To the one whose body is composed of ether, wind, fire, water, and earth; who is the form of the consciousness of Śiva;
and who is the sun that dispels the darkness of grief for all embodied beings. (2)
Salutations to Śiva, whose abode is at the root of a single mango tree. || 1 ||
That which is not space,
that which is not wind, that which is not fire, that which is not water,
that which is not earth, that which is not the full moon, and that which is not the sun.

Volition—that which causes the sacrificer to offer [oblations] for the sake of the body, which is the vessel for the soul; for those possessing bodies—that is, for those who have taken on physical forms; for the scorching of the darkness of grief—that is, for the removal of the darkness consisting of sorrow and suffering.

(I. 6a) For those who partake of a body—meaning for those who have assumed a physical form—for the purpose of burning away the darkness of grief—sorrow being suffering and darkness being that which obstructs [the light]. (2)
To the one who causes heat—the Sun;

(3) to the one whose abode is at the root of a single mango tree—*eka* meaning chief, *āmra* meaning mango tree, and *mūla* meaning root; to the one whose abode is at the foot of a mango tree—*nilaya* meaning a place of residence. (4) To the one who dwells there.
Salutation to Śiva—Ekāmranātha...
(5) ...namas! To him who is worshipped by Brahmā and all the gods, siddhas, and others through prostrations. (i. 6b)
Salutations to Śiva, whose lotus feet possess a majesty worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods;
who is eternally engaged in the performance of the duties of Brahmā and the rest;
and whose abode is at the root of the single mango tree.
"Brahmādi" refers to Brahmā, the gods, and the modalas; "sarvā" refers to all [of them]; "surā" refers to the deities;
and "siddhā" refers to the perfected beings (*siddhapuruṣa*).
To her who is well-worshipped—by the excellent crown worn by those who worship with devotion (i.
7a); to her who is praised by Brahmā and others—the gods beginning with Brahmā; to her who is venerable—worthy of salutation;
to her whose lotus-feet are auspicious.
For the sake of majesty—(3) [it is] the supreme, unsurpassed, and eternal life-force;
daily—every single day; Brahmā and the others—[those who] have reached the limit of the petals; duties—tasks; are to be conceived—should be arranged. (i. 7b)

*kṛteva*—to the one who has made the mountain of wealth contented; *namaśśivāya*, to Śiva whose abode is at the root of a single mango tree; *ekā*—the preeminent one; *māyirukkura* (2); *āmramūla*—at the base of the mango tree, which is a fruit-bearing tree; *nilayāya*—to him whose dwelling place is there; *māyidanṭattāyirukkura* (3); *śivāya*—to Śiva, the Lord of Ekāmra; *namaḥ*—salutations to him who performs prostration (4).
To the sun within the lotus-heart born from Dakṣa,
to the most beloved of Dāmodara, to the one higher than the highest. (I.8a)
Salutations to Śiva, the son of Dakṣa, who is devoted to the Praṇava mantra, and whose eternal abode is at the root of the Ekāmra tree. || 3 ||
To Pārvatī, daughter of Dakṣa; to the Lord who is the delight of the Goddess; to the Sun, the lotus of the heart;
and to Dāmodara, the Great Viṣṇu.
To the one who has made his abode at the foot of the primary *ekāmra* tree—the mango tree—(3);
to Śiva, who has established his residence at Ekāmranātha-purī; salutations! (4).
To him who is worshipped by devotees headed by Bāṇāsura;
to him who made Mount Sumeru into a bow;
to him who made the lotus-eyed one his arrow; to the destroyer of Tripura.
Salutations to Śiva, who dwells at the foot of the single mango tree.
(4) (2) To Him who is the source of joy for Bāṇāsura—Bāṇa, Asura, Nmoda, Lāna, and the foremost among them—the excellent thousand-fold hosts (3);
Having made [the mountain] into a bow—having fashioned the excellent bow-staff and the arrow-blade; [the mountain] Sumeru—[the mountain] Meru;
for the sake of the earth’s surface—for the sake of the surface of the world; having made it into an arrow—having fashioned the excellent arrow-blade;
for the lotus-eyed one—for Viṣṇu; of Tripura—for the demon Tripura.
Salutations to Śiva, the destroyer—He who has taken up residence at the root of the Ekāmra tree;
(4) "Ekā" means the principal one, and "Āmramūla" refers to the root of the mango tree. (5)
To the one whose abode is the mountain [Kailāsa]— the place called Ayidaḍaktāyirukkura— to Śiva— the Great Lord of Ekāmra—
at Himavat, salutations to the one who has made the moon and the Ganges his crest-ornament. (2)
Salutations always to Śiva, whose fame is equalized by the waters of the Bhāgīrathī, who possesses the eyes of the sun, the moon, and fire,
and whose abode is at the root of the Ekāmra tree. (3–5)

Bhāgīrathī—Gaṅgā; Śaśikalā—the digit of the moon (4); Kṛtā—she who has fashioned the golden fillet; Śekharāyā—she who is the ornament for the head (i.10 b). Bhāgīrathī—having come as Gaṅgā; Jalā—from the water; Samīkṛta—she who has leveled the golden fillet (2).
For the sake of glorification—glorification for him who possesses the most excellent form;
for Bharga—him who is the very embodiment of splendor (3).
Bhānu is the sun, Śaśin is the moon, and Vahni is fire (4).
For the sake of seeing—[the Lord] who dwells at the foot of the mango tree, to Śiva, the refuge, obeisance.

(I. 11a) "Ekā" means the principal; "māyi" means dwelling; "rūkkura" means [dwelling] at the root of a tree. "Āmramūla" means at the root of a mango tree (*cūtavṛkṣa*); "nilayāya" means to him whose abode is established there. (2)
For Śiva— the one from the sacred precinct of Ekāmranātha— salutations to him whose neck is resplendent with the brilliance of Hālāhala poison,
and to him whose chest is beautifully adorned with garlands. (3–4)

Salutations to Śiva, the destroyer of Manobhava, Kṛtānta, and Jalandhara, whose abode is at the root of the Ekāmra tree. (6) [He who is the source of the Hālāhala poison, the time of ten million Kalpas, and the supreme Viṣattu. (i. 11b)
O you who are adorned with a neck that possesses the brilliance of a radiant jewel,
O you who are beautiful with garlands,
O you whose speech is delightful and charming!
(4) With his chest adorned by a radiant pearl necklace;
and upon his chest—[he appeared] like the god of love, Manobhava, for the sake of Manmatha, and like Kṛtānta, Yama, for the sake of Yama. (i. 12a)
To the destroyer of the Jalandharas—the one who has swallowed the poison Hālāhala—to Śiva whose abode is at the root of Ekāmra; salutations to the one who has swallowed the preeminent Māyā. (3)
To the one who has made the root of the mango tree—*cūtavṛkṣa*—his abode—*nilaya*, meaning he has taken up residence there;
to Śiva—the Great Lord of Ekāmra; salutations (*namaḥ*) to him who is the elephant-faced, the six-faced, and engaged in dance. (i. 12b)
Salutations to Śiva, who stands at the side, who is served by a multitude of attendants on all sides,
who is dear to his devotees, who eternally removes the sins of worldly existence,
and whose abode is at the root of the Ekāmra tree. (7)
The elephant-faced one is Vighneśvara-roḍaya; the six-faced one is Subrahmaṇya-roḍaya; Nṛttā is Nāṭyattoḍe; Yuktā is Kuḍikoṇḍuyirukkura as stated;
Pārśva is Pakkattule; and she who stands there is Yirukkuratteoḍattānavarāyu. (i.13a)
Surrounded by—those equal to the *nāla* fruit; served by the hosts of the *gaṇas*, namely the *pramatha* hosts; beloved by his devotees, that is, dear to the devotees of Śiva;
the source of worldly existence (*bhava*).

To the one who removes sin—*pāpa-pāpattai*, meaning "he who dwells as the supreme remover of sins" (4); to the one whose abode is at the root of a single mango tree—*ekāmramūlanilayāya namaśśivāya*; "single" (*eka*) means "preeminent" (*mukhya*) (i.
13b), and "root of the mango" (*āmramūla*) means "the base of the mango tree" (*cūtavṛkṣamūla*), while "abode" (*nilaya*) means "one who has made that his place" (*sthānamāyidaḍaktāyi*) (2).
To Śiva—the lord of Ekāmranātha—salutations! Salutations to the five-faced one who liberates bound souls from their fetters, and who gazes with the side-long glance of the five eyes. (3–4)

Salutations to Śiva, the abode at the root of the Ekāmra tree, who bestows liberation upon those devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra. (8) To the Five-Faced One: — *Añji* means face; *mukha* means from the face; *te* means to you; *udatta* means elevated; *anavara* means unsurpassed; *āyuḥ* means life. *Paśu* means animal; *paśu-kala* means the nature of an animal; *oḍaya* means remove. *Pāśa* means the bond of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). (2)

For the sake of liberation— [I bow] to the five trees beginning with the *pokkaḍikkara* and the wish-fulfilling tree (*añjikalpavṛkṣa*); [I bow] to the primordial thousand trees and to the one who has cast his glance upon me.
For the sake of contemplation: "The five-syllabled [mantra] which bestows long life from the beginning" (I.14b);
"Recite"—for the purpose of reciting; "Supreme"—the most excellent life; "Beneficial"—that which brings about a favorable life. (2)
Salutations to Śiva, the bestower of liberation, the creator, the one who dwells at the root of the *ekāmra* tree. (3) *Ekā* means the preeminent form; *āmramūla* means the root of the mango tree.
To Nilaya—the one who has made this place his abode—(4);
to Śiva—the Lord of Ekāmra; salutations (namaḥ)—to Nāgeśvara, who is worshipped by the Vedas and Āgamas. (i. 15a)
Salutations to Śiva, who delights in the drama, who causes the nine kinds of grain to flourish, who always endures all manner of offenses,
who dwells at the root of the Ekāmra tree. (9)

To Nāgeśvara—[meaning] to the lord of serpents (*nāga-sarpa*)—and to Īśvara—the Lord (4)—who is the source of the *nigamas*, that is, the Vedas, and the source of the *āgamas*, that is, the Śaiva scriptures.
To Pūjitā—Pūjikkapaṭṭavarāyu; to Nāṭya—Nāṭyattule; to Priyā—Prītiyeoḍattānavarāyu (2); to Navadhānya—Navadhānyaṅgale;
to Vivardhanā—Vṛddhipaṇṇuravarāyu (3).
To one who wears various ornaments for various offenses, to the one who possesses a single excellent companion for endurance,
to Sadāśiva— the one who exists as Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, at all times (i. 16a).

Salutations to Śiva, whose abode is at the root of a single mango tree—*ekā* meaning the preeminent *māyi* tree, and *āmramūla* meaning the root of a mango tree; *nilayāya* means he whose dwelling is there;
(*namaḥ*) to Śiva—the Great Lord of Ekāmra. (3)
Salutations— by means of this prostration—
to the Lord of Kailāsa, who is enchanting to the Daughter of the Mountain, who bestows the true attainment of liberation, and who has the moon as his crest-ornament.
I meditate upon the Lord of the Single Mango Tree, the Great Lord, the enemy of Kāma and the destroyer of Time, within my heart.
To Kailāsa—unto Kailāsa; (2) to the Lord—the Master; to Girijā—the Goddess Pārvatī; to the Manohara—one who brings delight;
(3) to Kaivalya-mukti—the primary liberation.

"Pradam" means one who possesses a crest; "Ku...ravarāyu" (4), "Yinduśekharam" means one who bears the moon as a crest; "Indu-candranai" means with the moon as a crest; "Śekharam" means one who wears it; "Kālāntakam" means [the destroyer] of Kāla, that is, Yama.

Antaka—the life-force that causes destruction; Kāmaripu—the enemy of desire, the wind that subdues the god of love; Maheśa—the one who is the great lord; Ekāmranātha—the Lord of Ekāmra; in my heart—I meditate upon him with focused contemplation. (i.17a) (2) I contemplate him within my heart through the practice of dhyāna.
I bow to Śambhu, the Lord of Umā; I bow to the Preceptor of the Gods; I bow to the Cause of the Universe;
I bow to Him who is adorned with serpents and who holds a deer; I bow to the Lord of all beings. (4) I bow to Him whose eyes are the Sun, the Moon, and Fire; I bow to the Beloved of Mukunda.
I bow to the one who is the glory of his devotees, the giver of boons; I bow to Śiva, the benefactor. (i.
17b) The story of Śaṅkara’s life, whose essence is the flavor of narrative, has been proclaimed by the preceptor Candraśekhara. (2)
O Blue-throated One, may the service of your feet be mine in birth after birth!
(3) May there be ten million killings of Brahmins, and may there be ten million arrivals of those who have no refuge!
"O Mahādeva, by the chanting [of your name], they immediately attain dissolution.
(4) To Śambhu—I shall offer salutation; to Umāpati—to Pārvatīdevī, the consort—I shall offer salutation. To the Lord—I shall offer salutation. I shall offer salutation.
I bow to the Teacher of the Gods— the sole deity of the gods— and to the Supreme Guru,
the Lord who is the cause for the worlds.
I bow— saluting with prostration—
to Him who has serpents as His ornaments; I bow— saluting with prostration— to Him who holds a deer,
the supreme Lord who dwells upon the mountain.
I bow— offering salutation—
to the Lord of Beasts (paśūnām patiḥ), the Lord of those who are ignorant; I bow— offering salutation—
to Sūryā, who is also Sūrya.
Candrā—moon; Vahni—fire; Netram—eyes; Oḍattānavarai—having placed upon the head; Vande—I salute; Mukundapriyam—the beloved of Mukunda; Mukundā—of Mahāviṣṇu;
Priyam—the beloved.
I bow to the one who is praised by the most excellent of those seeking wealth;
I bow to the glory of the devotees, the glory of the devotees, the leader of the multitude of devotees; I bow to the one who is adorned with the crown of glory.

I bow— in offering salutations— to those who have committed millions (koṭayaḥ) upon millions (aneka-koṭi-kalūm) of Brahman-murders (brahmahatyānām)— meaning the killing of Brahmins— and who have committed millions upon millions of forbidden sexual acts (agamyāgamam), such as approaching their mothers and so forth.

"O Mahādeva" (i. 19b): "Mahādeva" means the Great God; "iti" means in this manner; "from the proclamation" (kīrtanāt) means by means of the act of proclaiming; "immediately" (sadyaḥ) means at that very moment; "the Lord" (prabhuḥ) refers to [Śiva] who destroys [suffering]; "they come" (āyānti) means they attain the state of being free from suffering.
Of Śaṅkara: *Sāmbaśivaroḍaya* (4),
*Caritā*— *Caritaṅgaloḍaya*, *Kathārasammuva*, *Candraśekharā*— *Candraśekharoḍaya* (i.20a), *Guṇāguṇaṅgaloḍaya*, and the hymn of praise (*kīrtanamum*), *Nīlakaṇṭhā*— *Oyi Sāmbaśivare* (2).
O Emboḍai, may service at Your feet—Your very toes—be rendered by me in birth after birth, throughout many lifetimes. (Ekāmranātha Śataka, i. 20b)
O Lord Śambhu, Your portion is the one named the illustrious Bhairava—the "Terrible One"—who has blood-red hair, who shines with camphor in His palm, and who is the conqueror of the three worlds;
under the guise of begging for blood, He [subdues] the proud hosts of the best of gods, headed by the illustrious Viṣṇu, who are devoid of true knowledge. (2-3)
May Dhūrjaṭi, who is skilled at removing their pride by piercing them with his trident, protect us from calamity.

(1) O Lord—O Creator of the World, O Āyirukkura; O Śambhu—O Sāmbaśivarē; you are my portion (*tvadaṃśaḥ*), you are my refuge (*tvad-ommoḍaya*), you are my share (*aṃśa-māyum*); [I have] crossed over [the world] with the palm of your hand (*karatalā-ullaṅkayyile*). (i. 21a)
Vilasat-prakāśin—shining brightly like camphor; Karpūra—camphor-like, possessing an unceasing radiance from his skull (2); Raktā—red like saffron; Keśa—hair like the dark blue sapphire (3);
Bhīma—terrible and fearsome; Tribhuvana-vijayī—the conqueror of the three worlds; Tribhuvanā—from the three worlds (4).

The victorious one—Rāyarūkkura, whose nature is victory; the one called Bhairava—Bhairava, who is known as Bhairavarāya (5); Peruṇḍānasvāmin; under the pretext of begging for blood—*rakta* meaning blood (*raktat-tunōḍa*) (i.21b), *bhikṣā* meaning begging (*bhikṣayennura*), and *chalena* meaning by means of a pretext (*vyājattunāle*); those devoted to me—those headed by Śrī Viṣṇu.
(2) To Mahāviṣṇu, who is the foremost among the great;
(3) to the best of the gods, the most excellent of deities, who agitates [the world]; (4) to those who possess a multitude of delusions, and to those who are arrogant, who are full of pride.
May Kāmeśa— who protects from all evils, who is endowed with desirable majesty, whose eyes are full of compassion,
whose body is marked by the bracelets on the breasts of Kāmākṣī, and who bestows both liberation and the fulfillment of desires— protect you.

I worship the sole Lord of lovers, whose lotus-feet are praised by the foremost of the gods, headed by Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci; whose face resembles the full moon, and who dwells most deeply within the heart.
(5) He is endowed with desirable majesty, [surpassing] the excellence of beauty and desirable majesty. (i. 22b)
(1) Endowed with the grace of Kuḍikoṇḍavarāyu; (2) filled with the compassion of Dayaināle; (3) whose glance is the sight of Oḍattānavarāyu;
(4) the abode of the goddess Kāmākṣī, [and] the bracelets upon her breasts.

Aṅkitā—[She] who is adorned with the cloth of the eightfold supernatural powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*); Kaivalyadā—the bestower of liberation (*mokṣa*); Kāmadā—the bestower of all desired objects; Indrā—she who is the consort of Indra, the lord of gods;

Upendrā—she who is the consort of Mahāviṣṇu; Viriñcā—she who is the consort of Brahmā, the creator; Mukhyā—she who is the foremost among all [goddesses]; Vibudhaiḥ—by the gods (*devatās*). (5) (i. 23a) (2)

Rudra—his bow, which is the fivefold arrow; Mahat—the greatness; Adbhuta—wonderful and marvelous;

The protector—Pokkaḍikkara Varāyu; consisting of sacred revelation—the one whose nature is the Vedas (5);

The pair of feet—those two feet which are the supreme refuge for the weary (2);
the true devotees—those who have churned the depths of the realization of knowledge (3);
surrounded by—those who have attained the highest state (4); with a face resembling the full moon—equal in splendor to the full moon (4).
In the face—at Oḍakkuttāyirukkura; (Ekāmranātha)—at Ekāmradhara-nātharai (5);
in the heart—at Hṛdayattūl; intensely—meditating upon Him; I worship—I perform meditation (upon Him). || 16 ||
To the one with the brilliance of pure crystal, the preceptor of the gods, the bestower of heaven and liberation,
who delights in protecting his devotees, who is higher than the highest, the destroyer of heretics,
who is eternal, free from disease, devoted to the goal, and the supreme ultimate beatitude— (I.42b).

I worship Mākandanātha, who bestows [boons] upon those endowed with faith and devotion. (17) (3) Śuddhā—she whose form is completely pure; Sphaṭikā—possessing the nature of crystal (4); Tejasaṃ—one who has attained the splendor of light; Suraguruṃ—the preceptor of the gods (5).

Bestower of heaven and liberation—he who grants the welfare of both heaven and mokṣa (I. 43a); beloved by devotees—he whose mind is intent on protecting his devotees; higher than the highest—he who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman (2);
destroyer of heretics—he who brings about the destruction of those hostile to Śiva (3).

(4) Nirantara—meaning constant; nityatvam—meaning the state of eternity; nirāmayam ca—meaning the absence of disease. (5) Uttamam—meaning the most excellent; niḥśreyasam—meaning liberation and auspiciousness; śraddhā—meaning that which is to be attained through faith.

To him who is endowed with devotion—meaning, to the one who possesses devotion—to that Mākandanātha, Ekāmbaranātha, who bestows grace upon those who approach him, I worship; that is, I shall meditate upon him. || 17 || (2)
The Lord, blazing with a body as radiant as ten million times ten thousand suns, who is incomparable in bestowing the highest good upon the wretched who seek refuge;
who sports with the foremost of his hosts whose fame pervades the quarters of space; the giver of bliss.
One should always meditate upon Śiva together with Ambā, who dwells at the root of the mango tree that is the essence of the Vedas. || 18 ||
Mārtāṇḍa—the Sun; having churned [it], [he attained] the life-span of ten thousand crores of *padmas*; *koṭikki*—of equal measure; *vapuṣā*—by means of his body (*śarīrat-tunāle*);
*jājvalyamānam*—blazing intensely; *prabhum*—the Lord (*prabhuvāyum*). (2) i. 44a)

To the poor—the destitute—to those seeking refuge—a shelter for those wandering in distress; incomparable—beyond all measure; the source of supreme bliss—the giver of ultimate welfare; in the act of bestowing—she who grants [all] things. (4)
Delighting—attached to life; pervaded by fame—spreading through the quarters of the sky;
in the quarters—in the intermediate spaces between the directions;
with the best of hosts—the lords of the Pramatha hosts; sporting—moving about playfully. (2) i.44b–45a)

(3) He spoke directly— that is, perceptibly— the giver of bliss, the bestower of contentment; (4) he is the embodiment of the Vedas, the essence of the Vedas, and the one who has brought forth the nectar of immortality.
I shall constantly meditate upon Mūlā—aḍiyai, whose abode—nilayaṃ—is the place of the Oḍattayirukkura tree, namely Sāmba-Ekāmranātha. (5) || 18 ||

O All-pervading Lord, whose feet are served by the lord of the hosts of spirits, who is skilled in both cursing and bestowing grace—[I seek refuge in You], who are intent on the path of worldly activity involving the expansion of thoughts and an inclination toward evil attachments; whose mind is agitated by anger; who moves along crooked paths; who is bent over merely to fill his belly; and who is hunched.
O Lord, beloved of Kāmākṣī, O jewel for protection, protect me, protect me with compassion!

(19) [He is] one who is attended by the lords of the hosts of *bhūtas*, who are capable (*dakṣa*) in both cursing and bestowing grace; [those] capable ones (*dakṣa*) are those who are proficient in both cursing (*śāpa*)—meaning they are able to curse—and bestowing grace (*anugraha*)—meaning they are able to grant grace;

and the lords of the hosts of *bhūtas* (*bhūtagaṇapaiḥ*) are the leaders of the *pramatha* attendants (*pramathagaṇādhipati-kalanālai*). [He is] one who stands having been served by them at his feet (*aṅghri*).
O All-pervading Lord, whose life-force is drawn from the feet;
O Beloved of Kāmākṣī, the vehicle of the Consort of Kāmākṣī; O Lord of Ekāmranātha; O Pāpātūla.
Attachment—clinging to the cooked; sleep—weighing upon the heart; worldly expansion—the arising of the manifold world (3);
sense objects—the clinging to objects; activity—the arising of the burden of duty; the path—the weighing of the way (4).

*Ratam*—addicted; *kopāt*—from anger; *ākulā*—becoming agitated; *mānasam*—the mind; *kupathagam*—going upon an evil path; *kukṣimbharam*—one who merely fills his belly; *kutsitam*—being censured; *mām*—me; *karuṇayā*—by means of compassion. (i. 46a)
Protect, protect—O protector of the protectors, O protector of the protectors! 19.

In the island named Jambū, measuring fifty crores of *yojanas* in extent, in the illustrious land called Bhārata— a beautiful king among regions renowned throughout the world— situated in the midst of the great bridge of the Snowy Mountains.
I take refuge in the good fortune of Umā, who has made her dwelling at the foot of a mango tree in Śrī-Kāñcī.
(5) [She who] churns fifty crores of Ambadas; she whose number is measured by a crore;
she who is limited by her own measure; she who shines brilliantly like a flame. (2)
yojana—measuring two yojanas; length and breadth—endowed with both dimensions; kūḍikkoṇḍu yiṟukkuṟa (3);
in this—here; named Jambū—the one known as Jambū (4).
In the island—at Dīpattule; at Śiśiragiri—at Himotparvata;
at Setu—at Rāmeśvara; in the middle—at Naḍuvile.
In the praiseworthy—[the land] of Śreṣṭhamāyirukkura (6);
in the one called Bhārata—the Bharatamennu Pereoḍayattāyirukkura; in the year—Varśattule; renowned—famous (i. 47a); on earth—in the land; shining—manifesting itself; Kṣetrarāja—the holy field.
Rāja—Prakāśicci Koṇḍuyirukkura; Cūtamūle—Cūtā-Māmarattunoḍaya; Mūle—Verile; Kṛtā—Paṇṇapaṭṭuyirukkura;
Vasati—Sthānatteoḍattāyirukkura (5);
Umā—Kāmākṣīdevi; Bhāgadeya—Daivamāna Ekāmranātharai (6).
I take refuge in meditation, O Paṇṇura. || 21 ||
Praised by Indra, the enemy of Jambha; honored by Agastya, who delights in the sacred scriptures;
constantly gratified by the dance of celestial beauties such as Rambhā;
and surrounded by hosts of great lords of yogis born from the mind of the Lotus-Seated One.
I worship the sole Lord of Āmravana, who dwells on the banks of the Kampa and is known in the heart as the other [Lord].
(3) Praised by the enemy of Jambha—the Lord of Devas—this hymn of praise, composed upon a precious leaf of gold, is [endowed with] prosperity. (4) Śrī...
*Tāvanarataṃ* means "resorted to by those who have taken refuge in the stages of life (*āśramin*)";
*avanā* means "protection" (*rakṣikā*); *rataṃ* means "attached to life" (*āsaktarāyu*); *kumbhodbhavārādhitaṃ* means "worshipped by Kumbhodbhava," where *kumbhodbhava* refers to Agastya.
(2) He was propitiated—meaning he was honored—with excellent garments such as *rambhā* and other fine cloths;

(3) by the celestial beauties—the maidens of the world of the gods—with *lāsya*, meaning with dance; (4) he was satisfied—meaning he was made to experience satisfaction—with [gifts] such as excellent garments.
Born from the lotus-throne of the god Brahmā (5), born from the lotus-stalk of Mānasa; the great one (mahā) among those who possess the great qualities (mahattukkalāyirukkura) (i. 48b);
the lord of yogins (yogīndra), O you who are surrounded by hosts (vṛndaiḥ) of sages (samohaṅgaloḍe) (2).
Surrounded by Aḍikoṇḍavarāyu; residing on the banks of the Kampa, [namely] Kampātīra and Kampātīrattūle; residing at Vāsaṃpaṇṇikoṇḍuyirukkara, [namely] Ekāmranātharai (3);
in the heart, [namely] Hṛdayattūle; crossing over (4).
I worship meditation upon the atom. || 21 ||
O Devaśrī, Kāmakoṭīramaṇa, Śiva, Mahādeva, the God of Gods and primordial deity;
O Lord Śrīkaṇṭha-Śambhu, victory, victory to you, O ocean of compassion, O infinite power!
O Sthāṇu, Lord of the Universe, whose hand shines with a bow more formidable than that of Viśvādhika!

O Lord Tripurāntaka, dweller of glorious Kailāsa, may your form accompanied by Ambā protect us. (i. 49a) O Lord, O Śrīkāmeśvara, O Śrī Kāmakoṭidevī, O Consort of the Supreme Ramana, O Śivā, O Śiva, O Mahādeva—may you be the sole deity for the gods. (3)
O Primordial One—[you who are] the principal deity;

O Lord—[you who are] the master Śrīkaṇṭha, the Sovereign; O You who possess compassion and mercy; O You whose power is as infinite as the ocean—[you who have arisen] from the ocean; O Infinite One—[you who are] immeasurable. (i. 49b)
O Śakti! You who are seated upon the serpent Oḍattāna; you who are Sthāṇu and Viśveśvara; you who are superior to the universe—*viśvādhikā*;
you who are *adhika*, meaning preeminent; you who reside within the hand (*karā*)—(3)—you who shine forth with splendor (*vilasat*).
On Mount Meru—at the peak of Mount Meru; with the bow—by means of the bow; Bhīmā—the terrifying one; Śrīmat Kailāsa—at the glorious Mount Kailāsa; Vāsin—residing;
Tripurahara—the destroyer of the demon Tripura.
O pervasive one, Yirukkura (i.
50a), O Sāmbamūrte—whose nature is that of Sāmba Śiva—O Ekāmranātha, victory, victory!
Protect me. || 22 ||
I bow to Bharga, adorned with serpents, Paśupati, the three-eyed purifier,
who is worshipped by the celestial sages Bhārgava, Vyāsa, Marīci, Gautama, Śuka, and Brahmā,
and who was gratified by propitiation with *arka*, *droṇa*, *subilva*, leaves, and flowers.
I worship Ekāmranātha, who bestows the station of the Lord of Heaven and is most dear to the heart.
(5) Bharga—He whose form is like the sun; Pannagabhūṣaṇam—one adorned with *pannagas*, that is, serpents; Paśupatim—the Lord of creatures, [the protector] of all creatures, beginning with humans. (2)
Pati—the Lord Vāyu;
Phālekṣaṇa—Netriyūle, whose eyes are like those of a cat; Oḍattānavarāyu (3);
Pāvana—the completely pure Rāyu; Bhārga—Bhṛgu, Vyāsa, Marīci, Gautama, and the others (4).
*Śukā*—the *śuka* flower;
*modalāna*—by the Brahman-sages (*brahmarṣi*); *brahmarṣigallanāle* (5); *pūjitam*—the *pūjika* flower; *arkā*—the *arka* flower; *droṇā*—the *tumba* flower (i. 51a).
With *bilva* leaves— the *bilva* leaf— with flowers— having garlanded with blossoms— with worship— performing adoration (2)—
having been praised— being satisfied— the Lord of Heaven— the Sovereign of the Gods— at his feet— at that place— gave— bestowed a boon.
I worship the Lord of Ekāmra, who is more dear than my own heart, with the lotus of my mind fixed in meditation. || 23 ||
O Guru, whose form is the ether beyond the supreme, higher than the five-fold Brahman-body;
by the rays of your slightly bent left foot, the [darkness] reddened like the morning sun has been shaken off.
[He who is] somewhat ignorant, possessing a deceptive human nature, and endowed with a heart of hardness.
To the one who is the most compassionate toward the ignorant, residing at Śrī Kāmakoṭi;

(2) whose body consists of the five Brahmans, [and] whose body is the supreme life-force of the five auspicious Brahmans; (3) [and] who is higher than the highest, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman. (4)

Having the nature of space (*ākāśasvarūpin*), having the nature of the arising of both space and the substance of space—by way of form, [it is] the supreme wind (*rūpatteḍattānavarāyuṃ*)—the teacher (*guru*), the wind of the teacher (*guruvāyuṃ*); "something" (*kiñcit*) means the sound *koñca*; "contracted" (*kuñcita*) means the drum-skin (*maḍakkapaṭṭu*) is struck. (i.52a)
(1) With rays rising at the time of binding the left foot—[the state] where the mass of light is subdued; (2) the "driven-out" [state], where the fierce brilliance is suppressed;
(3) the "morning-sun," which is the state of the rising sun at dawn.

*Kalpakataro*—one who possesses a life-span like that of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*). (4) *Śrīkāmakoṭi*—to the seat (*pīṭha*) of Kāmakoṭi. *Vate*—the Lord Ekāmranātha. (i. 52b) *Kiñcijñaṃ*—one who possesses little knowledge. *Gatapuruṣaṃ*—one who lacks capability or strength. *Kapaṭavān*—one who is full of deceit and fraud.
Hardness—hardness toward me; worry—worrying for my sake; endowed with—having taken upon himself; the fool—the wicked one; me—me; with compassion—with compassion; protect—protect me. || 24 ||
His face is like the orb of the full moon arising from the ocean of the nectar of bliss;

his form is pure wisdom, his body is half Umā, he is stainless, the soul of all, and the bestower of happiness. He is the object of meditation, endowed with indivisible non-dual consciousness, and intent on protecting the wretched.
I worship the Lord whose face resembles the full moon, who is most dear to the heart, and who is designated by the syllable Eka. || 25 ||
Ānandā—bring forth the bliss of Brahman; Amṛtasāgara—the ocean of nectar; Udbhavā—arising; Lasat—shining brilliantly; Pūrṇendu—the orb of the full moon (i.53b).

Ānana—the one whose mouth is the supreme life-force; Jñānākāra—the one whose nature is knowledge; Umārdhadeha—the one who has half his body as Umā (the Lord of Half-Woman); Amala—the one who is stainless and pure; Sarvākūta—the one whose form is the totality of the phenomenal world (3).
Śarmada—the bestower of happiness; Dhyāna—the object of meditation; Dhyeya—the one worthy of being meditated upon (4).

*Akhaṇḍā*—one who possesses a full moon; *vaibhavā*—one who is exceedingly majestic; *yutam*—one who has attained the supreme state; *dīnāvane*—the protector of the wretched; *dīnā*—those who are poor; *avane*—the one who protects them; *tatparam*—one who is intent upon that; *rākācandranibhānanam*—whose face resembles the full moon; *rākācandra*—the full moon; *nibhā*—one who is similar to; *ānanam*—the face.
— Having drawn [the deity] from his mouth into the tree (3), [I worship] Ekāmranātha; O Ekāmranātha, in the heart—within the lotus of the heart—I firmly declare (4): "I worship [Thee];
perform meditation [upon me]. || 25 ||

To the one known as Girīśa— whose neck is blue, whose crest is the moon, who holds the entire universe in his hand, whose weapon is the trident, whose chest is adorned with a girdle of serpents, and who has Mṛḍa and Sthāṇu as attendants— to him [I offer this],
for the sake of the boy whose mind is distressed, who is oppressed by the cravings of others, and who is deceitful.
May this [goddess] abide upon me, the tree that provides shade for the non-depressed kalpas, on the peak of Śrī-Kāmakoṭi.

(2) O you whose neck and throat are blue; O you who are adorned with the crescent moon as a crest upon your head; O you who have cast down all the hosts of Māyins; O you who are the life-force of all living beings. (3) O you who are the supreme one. (3) O you who are the destroyer of all illusions. O you who are the breath of life for all creatures.
Īśā—O supreme among lords of gods;
Śūlāyudhā—O you who hold the trident weapon; Vyālā—O Hara, whose garland is of serpents; Ākalpā—O you who destroy even the slightest of faults.
He who shines with splendor (lasat), who is the one who burns away the forest of sins (prakāśiccikoṇḍuyirukkura);

he who is the supreme one among those who have crossed over Māra (bhujāntarāmāre oḍttānavare); he who is the compassionate one (mṛḍā), who is the one who grants joy (mṛḍareyannum); he who is the immovable one (sthāṇo), who is the pillar-like one (sthāṇuvennum); he who is the lord of the mountains (girīśā), who is the husband of Pārvatī (pārvatīkki patiyennum); and he who is the imperishable one (avyayā), who is known as the one devoid of destruction (nāśarahitarennum)—thus they recognize him. (1–3)

O Śrī Kāmakoṭīpati, O Ekāmranātha, who are like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) for the wretched—the poor; [to me] whose mind is "bālam"—that is, small or insignificant—and "vyākula"—that is, agitated or fickle. [This is] the state of the mind.
"Parajanā" means one who uproots other people (I. 55b); "drohā" means one who intends to harm; "abhibhūtam" means one who has been overcome; "śaṭham" means one who is cruel (2);
and "hyeyam" means one who is fit to be censured.
Protect me—O Lord, protect me!

(26) (3) Through service to Your lotus feet, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other guardians of the directions attain a divine, eternal abode of intense enjoyment, which is a refuge, a kinsman, and free from all evil. (4)
O Lord Mahāmākandānātha, whose face is serene, whose arms shine with the jewels from the sprout-like hoods of the serpent-king Sadbhoga, please cast aside my faults and protect me. 27.

"Your lotus feet" (tvatpādāmbuja); "your grace" (tvad-omudaya); "lotus feet" (pādāmbuja)—meaning those who reside at the lotus-feet; "by service" (sevayā)—meaning by means of service; "Druhiṇa"—Brahmā; "Mahāviṣṇu."
To Indra and the others—namely, to the guardians of the directions beginning with Indra; *divyam* means the fragrance of the gods; *śāśvatā* means that which bestows eternal life (4);
*bhogā* means for the sake of fortunes;
*gāḍhā* means being firm; and *nilayasthāna* means for the sake of a dwelling place (5).

The arms— those excellent arms of his— shine with a bond that is a friend to the world (bandhu-vāna-varāyu), possess a splendor that has reached the peak (sat-prakāśicci-koṇḍu-yirukku-ra), bear the hoods of the lord of serpents (bhogīndra-sarpa-śreṣṭhat-tuṇoḍa-ya), are adorned with gems (ratnā-ratnaṅ-gallu-nāle), and are marked by the presence of the divine bird (vilasat-prakāśicci-koṇḍu-yirukku-ra). (1–3)

*Prasannānanā*: *prasanna* means "clear" (*svaccha*), and *ānanā* means "face" (*mukha*); thus, it refers to one whose face is clear. (4) *Prabho*: [O] Lord (*prabhu*). *Mahāmākandanātha*: *mahā* means "supreme" (*śreṣṭha*), and *Mākandanātha* refers to Ekāmranātha. *Maddoṣaṃ*: [my] fault (*doṣa*). (i. 57a)
Having avoided—*pokkaḍicci*, me—*yannai*, and *kavā*—the protector. || 27 ||
I bow to Kālī, who raised her lotus-feet in the assembly to suppress Tāṇḍava’s arrogance; she who, with the fire born from her eye,
reduced the Triple City to ashes and constantly removes the suffering of the gods led by Indra.
I worship Mākandanātha, the eternal companion of Umā, who is ever-playful. || 28 ||

Kālī—Bhadrakālī; noḍaya—arise; tāṇḍavā—O you who perform the tāṇḍava dance; noḍaya—arise; khaṇḍanāya—for the sake of shattering; khaṇḍikkarattu poruṭṭu—[the one] with the severed head; sadasi—in the assembly; sabhayile—amidst fear; proḍvīkṛtā—exalted; mihavuṃ ośarayaḍukkapaṭṭuyirukkura—the one whose feet are placed upon the heads of those who have been struck down; aṅghriyaṃ bujaṃ—upon the lotus-feet; oḍattanavarāyuṃ—the one adorned with fresh garlands; nālikāsana—seated upon Brahmā; sārathiṃ—the charioteer; sārathiyāyi oḍattānavarāyuṃ—the one adorned with fresh garlands [placed] upon the charioteer.

With the fire produced from the friction of the eyes—the eyes of the one who has arisen—[the Lord] reduced Tripura to ashes; having thus turned it to dust, he did so perpetually. Thus, the gods, headed by Surendra, the chief of the lords of the gods, [were liberated]. (I.58a)

I worship, with constant meditation, the Lord who is the root of the tree of suffering that is the afflictions (kleśa), who is the destroyer of the great calamity of worldly existence, who is fond of play and attached to the erotic sentiment, who is accompanied by Umā— namely Śiva— who is the Lord of Mākanda— namely Ekāmranātha— at all times. (28) (5)
The Lord of Laṅkā, his body adorned with ten throats, exerted himself in pride to shake the glorious Silver Mountain with twenty unimpeded arms; yet,
due to the impact against the tips of the nails of your lotus-feet, he perished with his limbs shattered and broken.
O Lord of Śrīkaṇṭha and Gaurī, you have indeed arrived at the abode at the foot of the mango tree.

(29) The body (*tanuḥ*) of the ten-necked one (*daśakaṇṭha*), which was adorned (*śobhita*)— meaning it shone brilliantly (*prakāśiccikoṇḍuyirukkura*)— upon the necks of the ten-necked ones (*daśakaṇṭhāpattukaṇṭhaṃ gallunāle*), that body (*tanuḥ*)— meaning those limbs (*oḍattāna*)—
belonged to the Lord of Laṅkā, the Asura Rāvaṇa (*laṅkeśaḥ*).
With his feet—he who stands upon the twenty [fingers] (I.
59a); with his twenty [fingers]—he who stands upon the twenty [toes]; with his hands—the twenty-four [fingers]; the glorious Silver Mountain—Mount Kailāsa;
to move—it was impossible for anyone else.
With pride— that is, through the stalk of egoism— he made an effort— that is, he exerted himself— toward Your lotus feet— that is, toward the pair of Your lotus feet. (3–4)
(5) "Nikhā" means of one whose nails have been cut; "nuṇinoḍaya" means of one who has been pierced.

Due to the force of movement—meaning by means of being struck with a stone or the like—he is "chinnāṅgabhinnaḥ," meaning his limbs are severed and his body is split; "chinnā" means of one whose binding cloth has been cut; "aṅgā" means of one whose body has been [severed].
59b) Wounded— his limbs shattered, he was seized by the wise ones while suffering from the pain of being bound and stretched out. (2)
I meditate upon Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of Gaurī, the consort of Pārvatī, who dwells at the foot of a mango tree— Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of Ekāmra. (Thus one should contemplate him.)
O Śiva, Great Lord, may the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā, praise your auspicious nature which is endowed with blessings, and worship the dust of your feet—
the source of eternal happiness and the fulfillment of all activities such as stability and prosperity.
"Those who have attained the state of the auspicious word—let them now be addressed by Umā and Īśa.
(30) Śivā: O Śiva! O Maheśvara! O Maheśvara! You—O you who are free from delusion! Śīlam—let it be established (naḍatteyānadu).
[2] That which is joined with inauspiciousness; Amaṅgala—O you who are beyond the inauspicious! Yutam—let it be joined (kūḍikoṇḍadu). [3]
O Lord—O Master; from the worship of your lotus feet—your *om-mudrā*, [that is] the protection of your lotus feet (*aṅghri-kamala*);

from worship (*arcanāt*)—by means of ritual (*vidhi*), that is, through the grace of Brahmā and the other gods (*mukha*); Indra and the others—the deities beginning with the Lord of Gods (*indra*); the ancient ones—those of long standing (*cirantana*). (I. 60b)

Bringing happiness—bestowing happiness upon those with long lives; endowed with the means for performing all duties and activities while remaining in that state—having attained such a life and abiding therein; the state of supreme auspiciousness (3);
"supremely auspicious" (sumaṅgalā)—meaning bringing about welfare; "state" (padaṃ)—meaning a place; "how" (kathaṃ)—in what manner; "they have gone" (gatāḥ)—meaning they have entered.
O Lord of Umā and Pārvatī, tell me—that which is to be spoken to me.
(5) Salutations again and again to Your sandals; salutations again and again to Your jeweled anklets.
Homage, homage to your two lotus feet;
homage to the leaders of Kāñcīpura! || 31 ||

To Your feet— those which rest upon the lotus-like feet of Om Muḍayya— to the two sandals, the great ones, salutations again and again; to Your feet— those which rest upon the lotus-like feet of Om Muḍayya.
With the two anklets—*taṇḍai-kalaporuṭṭu*; "salutation after salutation"—*namo namaḥ*, meaning prostration;
with your two lotus feet—*ommuda-pādāravindaṅgale poruṭṭu*; "salutation after salutation"—*namo namaḥ*, meaning prostration. (5) (i.61b)
O Lord of Ekāñcīpura—O Ekāmranātha—to you—Omaku—(2)—let there be *namaḥ*—salutation—*astu*—may it be offered. || 31 ||
Having obtained a kingdom with an inexhaustible treasury accompanied by countless riches, surrounded by herds of elephants and horses, a home filled with sons, wife, friends, and cattle,
and endowed with incomparable enjoyments, as well as peerless fortune— having attained all this through your constant worship, it is unsurpassed.
Indeed, the gods, dānavas, and humans are content at the glorious Kāmakoṭīvatī.
"Accompanied by countless wealth" (i.62a): "Countless" means immeasurable; "wealth" means property;
"accompanied" means brought together.
The treasury—both the city of Paṇakoṭṭaḍi and that which was surrounded by herds of elephants and horses;
(3) the elephants—Ānaikaloḍaya, and the horses—Kudaraikaloḍaya; (4) by the herds—at Samohaṅgaloḍe.
Surrounded by—his kinsmen (*kūḍikkoṇḍu* and *yirukkura*), his kingdom (*rājya*) and his subjects (*rājyatteyum*) (5);
by sons, friends, wife, and cattle: sons (*putra*) are children (*pillaikaloḍe*); friends (*mitra*) are those bound by affection (*snehatāloḍe*) (i.62b);
wives (*kalatra*) are women (*strīkaloḍe*); and cattle (*paśu*) are livestock (*paśukkaloḍe*) (2).
Complete—meaning it will continue to delight people; endowed with enjoyments—meaning through good fortune;
possessed of—a house that shall stand firm for a long time (3); incomparable—meaning there is no equal to it;
and good fortune—meaning prosperity itself—[shall arise] through your worship—meaning by worshipping you (5).
*Nibhṛtam* means secretly; *sametya* means having approached; *santatam* means at all times; *Śrī-Kāmakoṭī-vate* refers to the Lord Ekāmranātha;
*devāḥ* refers to the gods who are the sole refuge of the deities.
The Dānavas—the Asuras—are not satisfied, nor are the humans—mankind; indeed, they are far from contentment. || 32 ||
Śiva, who is seated eternally upon the great, renowned, and exceedingly splendid mountain Meru— which is equal [in height] to the peak of Kailāsa and composed of gold near its base—
whose body bears the imprint of the circular marks from Kāmākṣī’s breasts, and who has the form of a great *liṅga*.
I worship the abode of compassion within the hearts of devotees. || 33 ||
Of Mahāmeru—of the mountain Mahāmeru (2);
equal to—having a similar extent (3); renowned—famous;
very great—of vast proportions.

In the abode—meaning in the vicinity of the Ālayattu; on the bank of the Kaṃpā—Kaṃpā being the Kaṃpā river, and *kūle* meaning on its shore; with golden mango trees—*kanakamayā* meaning made of gold, and *mākandā* meaning of the mango trees; nearby—meaning in the proximity.
"Constantly"— at all times— "seated"— having taken up residence—
(3) "Kāmākṣī"— the goddess Kāmākṣī— "her breasts"— the nipples of her breasts— and "her bracelets"— the rows of her bangles— (4).
Mudrā—marked with the seal upon the stalk; (i.

To the abode of compassion, the one who possesses compassion and mercy, the abode—meaning the place—of Śiva, namely Ekāmranātha, I bow with my heart; worship Him through meditation.
(33) [He is] bliss, non-duality, and indivisible consciousness.

I take refuge in Śiva, the protector of the distressed, who is consecrated by the crescent moon; he is attainable through meditation alone, the peerless tree, the sovereign of the root, and the bestower of liberation. (34)
Bliss—He whose nature is eternal bliss;
Non-duality—He who has cast away duality; Indivisible—He who is perfectly complete;
Consciousness—He whose nature is knowledge.
To the protector of the distressed; to the one who is like a lamp for the eyes of the poor and wretched;

to the initiated one, the most excellent among those who have received initiation; to the one who has the moon as his crest-ornament, the one upon whose head the moon is placed; to the one attainable through meditation alone, who is the primary object of meditation.

I take refuge in— that is, I serve— the one who is attainable, the lord of the root of the single mango tree (*ekacūtāśreṣṭha*), the supreme master of the root of the immortal *Āmarattu* (*mūlādhipati*), the bestower of liberation (*mokṣaprada*), the auspicious Lord of the Single Mango Tree (*Ekāmranātha*). || 34 ||
Untainted, eternal, of inconceivable majesty, ancient, a mass of consciousness, the immutable Lord,
consisting of the supreme ether, higher than the highest.
I take refuge in the lotus of the heart, adorned with the auspicious bracelets.

Nirañjana—He who is without any connection to the world of becoming; (5) Nitya—He who is eternal; Atarkyavaibhava—He whose glory is inconceivable, meaning He whose power and majesty are beyond the reach of thought; (i.66a) Cirantana—The Primeval Person, who is without beginning. (2)
The mass of consciousness (*cidghana*)—*cit* meaning knowledge, *ghana* meaning full; the Lord (*īśa*)—the Lord of lords (*īśvara*);
the imperishable (*avyaya*)—that which is devoid of destruction; the supreme (*para*)—the most excellent; consisting of the supreme ether (*parākāśamaya*)—having the nature of the supreme ether. (4)
The supreme among the supreme— the best of forms and the best of lifespans—
Śrīvalayāṅka (the Lord marked by the auspicious bracelet), who resides upon the heart-lotus of Ekāmranātha, which is like a lotus placed upon the chest. (2)
Regarding the basis: meditation [is practiced] on the sixfold atom. || 35 ||
I worship the eternal Sāmba, the crusher of the bodiless god of love, the one free from disease and stainless, the Lord of Ambikā,
whose lotus feet are worshipped by Janārdana.
One should always worship the wish-fulfilling tree with these names. || 36 ||
The eternal one—possessing everlasting life; Sāmba—possessing life accompanied by Ambikā (I.67a);
the destroyer of Anaṅga—the destroyer of the god of love; the healthy one—possessing life free from affliction; the stainless one—possessing pure life; (the Lord of Ambikā).

To Pārvatī’s husband, the lotus-feet of Janārdana, who is worshipped by Mahāviṣṇu himself; [the feet] which are the source of all that is prayed for and the source of all that is offered in worship; the lotus-feet upon which [all beings] have taken refuge. (i.67b)
To the wish-fulfilling tree for those who bow—
*nata* meaning those who offer salutation, and *kalpapādapa* meaning one whose nature is like the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), namely Ekāmranātha—
to him, daily, every single day.
I bow down— I offer my salutations—
to him whose crest is adorned with the crescent of the Gaṅgā moon,
and who is served by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas. (36) (3) (4)
I contemplate within my heart the Lord whose complexion is as white as camphor, who wanders upon the banks of the Kaṃpā, and who destroys the impurities of the Kali age.
(37) Gaṅgā—She is like a female elephant; Śaśāṅkaśakalā—She is like the crescent moon; Añcitā—She is like a beautiful woman. (2)
(3) His crown-region was adorned with a most excellent garland;
(4) he was being served by Gandharvas from among the Gandharvas, Kinnaras from among the Kinnaras, and Mahoragas from among the serpent-kings. He was attended by a supreme assembly of servants.
On the bank of the Kampā—on the shore of the Kampā river; dwelling—at Veḷḷūr; in the Kali age—in the dawning of the Kali Yuga;
destroying impurity—the remover of sin.
Karpūra—Paccakarpūrattuvel (3); Gauram—the Ekāmranātha of Velutuyirukkura; Citte—in the mind (4); Kalayāmi—I perform meditation (dhyāna) for a moment (paṇṇure). || 37 ||
Through the embrace of the daughter of the mountain king,
Maheśa contracts his own left body;
he who dwells on Mount Kailāsa and destroys the impurities of the Kali age.
I meditate incessantly upon the Lord of Kāñcīpurī in my heart. (i.
69a) Śailādhirāja—Śaila means mountain; Adhirāja means lord.
Himavat—the son of the mountain; Tanayā—the daughter, Pārvatī Devī. (2–3)

By means of embracing—[the state of] the reddish stalk of the hips; contracting—the [state of] the soft cloth-like skin; one's own—...; the left—the [state of] the curved [bone]; the body—the [state of] the thinness of the limbs. (i.69b)
Maheśam—the Great Lord; kailāsaśailāt—from Mount Kailāsa;
nilayam—whose abode is there;
kali—in the Kali age; kalmaṣaghnām—who destroys sins; yirukkura—he shines forth.
I meditate— through contemplation— upon the Lord of Kāñcīpura, Ekāmranātha, the sovereign of the city of Kāñcī, in my heart at all times. || 38 ||
The Lord of the Gods, with a smiling face and a blue throat,
seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), with hair like clouds,
served by Viriñci and others, and far removed from those of evil intent.
I ever praise Sadācūta Maheśa. || 39 ||
Smerā—beautifully radiant; ānanaṃ—the face, which is reddish-yellow; nīlā—dark blue; galaṃ—the neck, which is reddish-yellow. (i. 70b) ... (the hair).
— …., ….. (in the heroic posture)— equal to the royal throne (2),
the lotus posture— standing— Yirukkuravarāyu, with cloud-like hair— cloud— the sky.
(3) Keśaṃ-talamayirāyi means "having bound [it] with a cloth";
(4) vīrādibhiḥ means "by Vīrabhadra and others";
sevyaṃ means "to be served"; apatvacittā means "for one who lacks a resolute intellect."
I shall always (2), at all times, praise (īḍe)—that is, offer hymns of praise—to Dūrakāṇapaṭāvarāyu, who dwells upon the mountain, and to Cūtamaheśa, whose name is Ekāmrānātha. || 39 ||
Non-dual, stainless, and utterly pure;
fulfilling the desires of the Self, realized by all as the Self;
eternally pure, and bestowing the powers of *aṇimā* and the rest.
I take refuge in the Lord, who consists of the pure reality (śuddhatattva).
(40) He is without a second—unique...; stainless—having a perfectly pure life-force (rāyu);
one whose desires are fulfilled—having a life-force enchanting by its own will; ...—the destroyer of the afflictions (kali) of all living beings.

*Bhāvitaṃ*—meditation (*dhyāna*) which is the supreme life-force of the yellow silk band; *nityapūtaṃ*—the life-force that is eternally pure; *aṇimādi*—the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*) and so forth;
*modalāna*—(3) *bhūti*—prosperity; *daṃ*—the supreme life-force of the *kuḍukka* [sandalwood];
*śuddhatatva*—*śuddhā*—free from *māyā*; *tatvā*—having the nature of knowledge consisting of reality (*tatvamaya-jñāna*); *īśaṃ*—Lord Ekāmranātha. (i. 72a)
In the refuge—may they serve. || 40 ||
Having shaken off the entire web of karma through meditative absorption, beloved by the people yet invisible to the wicked,
[he is] the supreme among sages, the restrainer of the vital breaths and so forth.
I bow to the Lord of the Mango tree who dwells in the heart. || 41 ||
Dhyānā—she who is the essence of meditation; Vadhūtā—she who wears the ascetic’s upper garment; Akhilā—she who possesses all things; Karma—she whose limbs are action;
Jālā—she who is covered by a net of delusion.

For people—for those who are like a forest of wild beasts; for the beloved one—the most excellent life; by wicked people—by those most sinful forest-dwellers; invisible—to one who is blind from birth; vital breath and so forth—those that obstruct the movement of the breath and the rest; the best of yogis—the most eminent among practitioners of yoga. (I.73a)

I bow down— to offer salutation— to the Lord of the Single Mango Tree (Ekāmranātha), who resides in the heart— the abode within the lotus of the heart— and who possesses a body as delicate as a young mango sprout. || 41 ||

Through the hearing of the Vedanta and various refinements of the meaning of the true scriptures, the knowledge of reality is attained; by the enjoyment of worldly existence, you [cross] the ocean of becoming. (4)

Having led [them] away and caused them to cast off the impurities accumulated over many births, they have attained the state of Śiva; O Blessed One, O Lord Sāmbaśaṅkara, O Cūteśa, salutations to you! (42) (i. 73b) [Salutations to you who are the] upholder of the essence of the Vedānta scriptures... (2)
Through hearing and so forth— by means of the various methods (*vidhayaḥ*) such as the *kelakkaradumudalānānadugallanāle*—
and by thoroughly churning the Vedānta texts, which are the true scriptures (*sacchāstra*).
Having attained the knowledge of reality— the knowledge of Brahman— through the purification of the objects of the senses by means of discernment, [he] reached [the goal].

...those [beings], having emerged from delusion, with devotion— that stalk of devotion— at the feet— the toes— having led [them] across the ocean of existence (saṃsāra-samudra), the one holding the staff (dāṇḍī), through many births— that stalk of auspiciousness consisting of many lifetimes— (2).
Having abandoned the impurity accumulated through the performance of ritual acts—having cast it away—they have attained the state of Śiva, that is, the nature of Śiva; they have reached it. (3–4)
Truly blessed are we—
O Sāmbaśiva Śaṅkara, O All-pervading Lord, O Lord of the Single Mango Tree (Ekāmranātha), O Omakku— to You, salutation! || 42 ||
